content.meta_title: Achilles Tendinitis - Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
h1_titles: Achilles Tendinitis - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Achilles Tendinitis: Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Achilles tendinitis is an overuse injury of the Achilles tendon, the band of tissue that connects calf muscles at the back of the lower leg to your heel bone. It most commonly occurs in runners who have suddenly increased the intensity or duration of their runs. It's also common in middle-aged people who play sports, such as tennis or basketball, only on the weekends.

sections.heading: What is Achilles Tendinitis?
content: Achilles tendinitis is an overuse injury of the Achilles tendon, the band of tissue that connects calf muscles at the back of the lower leg to your heel bone. It most commonly occurs in runners who have suddenly increased the intensity or duration of their runs. It's also common in middle-aged people who play sports, such as tennis or basketball, only on the weekends.

sections.heading: Common Symptoms of Achilles Tendinitis
content: Pain and stiffness along the Achilles tendon in the morning
Pain along the tendon or back of the heel that worsens with activity
Severe pain the day after exercising
Swelling that is present all the time and gets worse throughout the day with activity

sections.heading: Causes
content: Sudden increase in the amount or intensity of exercise

sections.heading: Key Risk Factors
content: Medical conditions such as psoriasis or high blood pressure

sections.heading: Prevalence
content: Achilles tendinitis is very common, especially in runners and athletes.

Choose appropriate footwear

content: Acne is a chronic skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become plugged with oil and dead skin cells. It causes whiteheads, blackheads, pimples, nodules, and cysts. Acne commonly appears on the face, forehead, chest, upper back, and shoulders. While it primarily affects teenagers, it can occur at any age.

sections.heading: Treatment

Common Symptoms of Acne
Whiteheads (closed plugged pores)
Blackheads (open plugged pores)
Pimples (papules)
Pustules (papules with pus)
Nodules (large solid painful lumps)
Cystic lesions (painful, pus-filled lumps)

Causes
Excess sebum production
Hair follicles clogged by sebum and dead skin cells
Bacteria (Cutibacterium acnes)
Hormonal changes
Inflammation

Diagnosis
Physical examination of skin
Skin culture if bacterial infection suspected

Treatment
Topical treatments (benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, retinoids, antibiotics)
Oral antibiotics
Hormonal therapies (oral contraceptives, spironolactone)
Isotretinoin (for severe acne)
Procedures (chemical peels, laser therapy, drainage)

Key Risk Factors
Hormonal changes (puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy)
Certain medications (corticosteroids, testosterone)
Diet (possibly high-glycemic foods, dairy)
Stress
Family history

Prevention
Wash skin gently twice daily
Use oil-free, water-based makeup
Remove makeup before bed
Shower after sweating

h1_titles: Alopecia Areata - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Alopecia Areata: Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disease that causes hair loss on the scalp, face, and sometimes other areas of the body. Blood loss (heavy menstrual bleeding or bleeding from the gut)
Infections such as malaria or other chronic infections
Chronic diseases or inherited blood disorders

Evaluation for blood loss or infection
Assessment for chronic disease or inherited conditions

Treatment of infections or chronic disease

h1_titles: Ankylosing Spondylitis - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Ankylosing Spondylitis: Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis that primarily affects the spine. It causes inflammation of the spinal joints (vertebrae) that can lead to severe, chronic pain and discomfort. In more advanced cases, this inflammation can cause new bone to form on the spine, causing the spine to fuse in a fixed, immobile position, sometimes creating a hunched-forward posture.

sections.heading: Common Symptoms of Ankylosing Spondylitis
content: Pain and stiffness in the lower back and hips, especially in the morning and after periods of inactivity
Pain and swelling in other joints such as the shoulders, hips, knees, and feet

sections.heading: Causes
content: Unknown, but genetic factors are involved
HLA-B27 gene is present in most people with this condition

sections.heading: Prevention
content: Exercise and physical therapy can help manage symptoms

sections.heading: Prevalence

content.meta_title: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) - Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
h1_titles: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS): Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system produces abnormal antibodies against phospholipids — a type of fat — in the blood. APS can cause blood clots to form in arteries and veins, as well as pregnancy complications such as miscarriages and preterm births. It may occur alone or with another autoimmune disease such as lupus.

sections.heading: What is Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)?

It may occur alone or with another autoimmune disease such as lupus.

sections.heading: Common Symptoms of Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)
content: Lacy, net-like purplish skin rash (livedo reticularis)

sections.heading: Causes
content: Autoimmune antibodies (antiphospholipid antibodies: anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant)
May be triggered by infections, medications

sections.heading: Diagnosis
content: Blood tests for antiphospholipid antibodies (twice at least 12 weeks apart)

sections.heading: Key Risk Factors
content: Having lupus or another autoimmune disease

sections.heading: Prevalence
content: APS occurs in about 1–5% of the general population; seen in 15–20% of people with recurrent miscarriages.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system produces abnormal antibodies against phospholipids — a type of fat — in the blood. Common Symptoms of Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)
Blood clots in legs (DVT)
Blood clots in lungs (pulmonary embolism)
Stroke
Repeated miscarriages
Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia)
Lacy, net-like purplish skin rash (livedo reticularis)
Headaches or migraines

Causes
Autoimmune antibodies (antiphospholipid antibodies: anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant)
May be triggered by infections, medications

Diagnosis
Blood tests for antiphospholipid antibodies (twice at least 12 weeks apart)
CBC
Clotting tests

Treatment
Blood thinners (anticoagulants: warfarin, heparin)
Low-dose aspirin
Hydroxychloroquine
Statins

Key Risk Factors
Having lupus or another autoimmune disease
History of blood clots
Family history

Prevention
No direct prevention
Careful management of anticoagulation therapy

Prevalence
APS occurs in about 1–5% of the general population; seen in 15–20% of people with recurrent miscarriages.

Autoimmune/Rheumatic

h1_titles: Avascular Necrosis (Osteonecrosis) - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Avascular Necrosis (Osteonecrosis): Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Avascular necrosis, also called osteonecrosis, is bone death caused by reduced blood flow to the bone. When blood doesn't reach bone tissue, the bone begins to die and may eventually collapse. The hip is the most commonly affected joint, but avascular necrosis can also occur in the knee, shoulder, ankle, and wrist.

What is Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)?
Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a chronic pain condition that most often affects a limb (arm, leg, hand, or foot) after an injury. CRPS is characterized by prolonged or excessive pain and changes in skin color, temperature, and/or swelling in the affected area. There are two types: CRPS-I (without confirmed nerve injury) and CRPS-II (with confirmed nerve injury, formerly called causalgia).

Continuous burning or throbbing pain
Sensitivity to touch or cold (allodynia)
Swelling of the painful area
Changes in skin temperature (alternately sweaty and cold)

Changes in skin texture
Hair and nail growth changes
Joint stiffness and swelling
Muscle spasms and weakness

Injury or trauma (fracture, surgery, sprain)
Nerve damage or dysfunction
Abnormal inflammatory response
Abnormal interaction between central and peripheral nervous systems
In some cases, no clear precipitating event

Clinical examination using Budapest Criteria
Bone scan
X-rays
MRI
Sympathetic nerve blocks (diagnostic response)
Thermography

Physical and occupational therapy
Psychotherapy
Medications (antidepressants, anticonvulsants, corticosteroids, opioids)

Spinal cord stimulation
Intrathecal drug pumps
Mirror therapy
TENS

Female sex
Age 40–70
Previous fracture or injury
Immobilization after injury
Possible genetic predisposition

Prevention

Early mobilization after injury
Prompt treatment of pain after injury

Slowly progressive weakness in finger flexors (difficulty gripping)
Weakness in the quadriceps (difficulty getting up from a chair or climbing stairs)
Foot drop
Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing, in up to 60%)
Frequent falls
Asymmetric muscle involvement

Causes
Combined inflammatory and degenerative process
Protein aggregates within muscle fibers (amyloid deposits)
Possible autoimmune component (anti-cN-1A antibodies)

Physical examination
Blood tests (CK elevated — often mildly)
EMG
MRI of muscles
Muscle biopsy (rimmed vacuoles, protein inclusions)
Anti-cN-1A antibody testing

No effective disease-modifying treatment currently
Physical and occupational therapy (most important)
Dysphagia management
Assistive devices and fall prevention
Clinical trials ongoing

Key Risk Factors
Age over 50
Male sex (slightly)
HLA-DR3 association

Prevention
No known prevention

Estimated incidence 1–71 per million per year; increases significantly with age.

Joint pain and swelling (often lower extremities)
Spinal pain and stiffness
Sacroiliac joint pain

Eye inflammation (uveitis)

Autoimmune — shared inflammatory pathways between gut and joints
Gut bacteria translocating and triggering immune response

Clinical evaluation in context of IBD diagnosis
X-ray or MRI of spine and sacroiliac joints
Blood tests (inflammatory markers, HLA-B27)

Treating underlying IBD (TNF inhibitors helpful for both)

Sulfasalazine
Physical therapy

Having IBD (Crohn's or UC)
HLA-B27 positivity for spinal involvement

No specific prevention; controlling IBD may reduce joint manifestations

Peripheral arthritis in 5–20% of IBD patients; axial disease in 3–10%.

Genetic predisposition

Introduction
Psoriasis is a chronic, autoimmune skin disease that speeds up the skin cell life cycle, causing cells to build up rapidly on the surface of the skin. The extra skin cells form scales and red patches that can be itchy and sometimes painful. Psoriasis tends to go through cycles, flaring for a few weeks or months, then subsiding.

What is Psoriasis?
Psoriasis is a chronic, autoimmune skin disease that speeds up the skin cell life cycle, causing cells to build up rapidly on the surface of the skin. The extra skin cells form scales and red patches that can be itchy and sometimes painful. Psoriasis tends to go through cycles, flaring for a few weeks or months, then subsiding.

Red patches of skin covered with thick, silvery scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed or itch
Itching, burning, or soreness
Thickened, pitted, or ridged nails

Causes
Autoimmune — immune system triggers overproduction of skin cells
Genetic factors (family history in ~30%)

Biopsy (rarely needed)

Family history

Smoking
Obesity
Certain medications
Infections (streptococcal)

Moisturize skin
Avoid triggers (stress, skin injury, infection)

Limit alcohol

h1_titles: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS) - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS): Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a group of disorders that occur when the blood vessels or nerves in the space between the collarbone and first rib (the thoracic outlet) become compressed. This can cause pain in the shoulders and neck and numbness in the fingers. There are three types: neurogenic (most common), venous, and arterial TOS.

sections.heading: What is Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)?
content: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a group of disorders that occur when the blood vessels or nerves in the space between the collarbone and first rib (the thoracic outlet) become compressed. This can cause pain in the shoulders and neck and numbness in the fingers. There are three types: neurogenic (most common), venous, and arterial TOS.

sections.heading: Common Symptoms of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)
content: Numbness or tingling in the fingers (especially ulnar nerve distribution)
Blood clots in upper extremity veins (Paget-Schroetter syndrome)

sections.heading: Causes
content: Anatomical defects (cervical rib, tight scalene muscles)

sections.heading: Treatment
content: Physical therapy (posture correction, scalene muscle stretching)
Botulinum toxin injections into scalene muscles
Surgery (rib resection, scalenectomy) for refractory or vascular TOS

sections.heading: Key Risk Factors
content: Trauma to the neck or shoulder

sections.heading: Prevalence
content: Neurogenic TOS affects approximately 3–80 per 1,000 people; true prevalence uncertain.

Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a group of disorders that occur when the blood vessels or nerves in the space between the collarbone and first rib (the thoracic outlet) become compressed. Common Symptoms of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)
Numbness or tingling in the fingers (especially ulnar nerve distribution)
Neck, shoulder, and arm pain
Weak grip
Swelling of the arm (venous TOS)
Arm that changes color (venous/arterial TOS)
Blood clots in upper extremity veins (Paget-Schroetter syndrome)

Causes
Anatomical defects (cervical rib, tight scalene muscles)
Poor posture
Repetitive overhead activities
Trauma (whiplash, fall)

Diagnosis
Physical examination (provocative tests: Adson, Roos)
Nerve conduction studies
Imaging: X-ray, MRI, CT angiography
Doppler ultrasound

Treatment
Physical therapy (posture correction, scalene muscle stretching)
NSAIDs
Botulinum toxin injections into scalene muscles
Surgery (rib resection, scalenectomy) for refractory or vascular TOS

Key Risk Factors
Cervical rib
Poor posture
Repetitive overhead activities
Trauma to the neck or shoulder
Female sex

Prevention
Maintain good posture
Strengthen shoulder and neck muscles
Ergonomic workstation setup

Prevalence
Neurogenic TOS affects approximately 3–80 per 1,000 people; true prevalence uncertain.

h1_titles: Vitiligo - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention
Vitiligo: Overview

sections.heading: Introduction
content: Vitiligo is a long-term skin condition characterized by patches of the skin losing their pigment. The patches of skin affected become white and usually have sharp margins. The hair from the skin may also become white. Vitiligo is caused by a loss of melanocytes, which are cells responsible for skin pigmentation. It can affect people of any race or skin tone but is more visible in people with darker skin.

sections.heading: Common Symptoms of Vitiligo
content: Patchy loss of skin color (usually first appears on sun-exposed areas)
Premature whitening or graying of hair, eyebrows, eyelashes
Loss of color in the tissues that line the inside of the mouth and nose (mucous membranes)
Loss of or change in color of the inner layer of the eye (retina)

sections.heading: Causes
content: Possible triggers: sunburn, emotional stress, exposure to certain chemicals

content: Personal or family history of autoimmune diseases (thyroid, type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata)

content: Sun protection to prevent sunburned vitiligo patches

content: Affects about 0.5–2% of the global population; approximately 3.5–4 million Americans.
